author: Miles_Brundage
text: @paul_scharre Agree more/less is too simplistic, but more/less *at the current rate of abuse* is a coherent question, especially if it is difficult to filter the good from the bad. I claim that the good significantly outweighs the bad, and that a general decline would therefore be bad.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @EBKania If anything visa-related is a "weapon" in global innovation (though zero-sum thinking is super problematic as applied to science), it's the United States's historical openness to foreign researchers, which brings new ideas/perspectives and augments our very bad STEM pipeline.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @EBKania ...and that starts with recognizing that China is by far the biggest source of foreign PhD students, and that from a competitiveness perspective, visas are vastly under- rather than over-supplied currently--the US gets massive benefits from research happening within its borders.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Also, as folks who have looked at these issues such as @EBKania have noted, one can be concerned about/act on misuse of visas without overreacting and throwing the baby out with the bathwater. To make progress, though, politicians need a semi accurate mental model of US science..

author: Miles_Brundage

author: Miles_Brundage
text: We look forward to continued engagement as we move towards a final decision on the largest version of GPT-2 in the coming months! (7/7)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: As discussed in our recent report ( https://t.co/dx07wlGCFT), staged release is one approach to approaching responsible publication in AI & analyzing impact iteratively across model sizes. Further work is needed to improve processes and decision-making frameworks. (6/7)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: It is unclear how to coordinate releases in AI. We’ve called responsible AI development a collective action problem:  https://t.co/cKrzUC38Ab We’re excited by the coordination we've seen and think the AI community can do even better in the future with new tools/concepts. (5/7)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: A tricky issue about replication is how to weigh talent, compute, algorithms, data, and other factors. The GPT-2 case makes clear, IMO, the critical importance of compute as an input to examine carefully in this context. (4/7)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: In the last six months, we've coordinated with several replicators, and various technical developments (such as GROVER) helped bring GPT-2 within reach of a larger set of actors. We asked that communication be with our Policy team (languagequestions@openai.com) (3/7)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: In our first GPT-2 blog post, we noted that researchers could replicate our results, but that our approach would limit the initial replicators, prevent malicious use, and enable more time for discussion and impact analysis. (2/7)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Given recent discussions of GPT-2 replication, I thought it'd be good to clarify some of OpenAI's general thinking on the issues of publication norms, compute, and staged release. (1/7)

text: @lizjosullivan @axon_enterprise We definitely did not conclude that accuracy would address all concerns! Indeed we say the opposite, though definitely understand the concern around ethics washing!

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Those to-do's notwithstanding, I'm thrilled about all of the progress we *have* made and look forward to seeing others build on both the process and substance of our work.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: And there is a big space of face recognition technologies and applications beyond "face matching on body cameras," which is perhaps one of the more obviously-bad-today use cases (cf. others we discuss). Again, much more to be done on the board + beyond.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Finally, it's worth emphasizing that this report does not settle all the issues that we are concerned about, or that others are. For example, more work will be needed to get anything like a consensus on the board about what to do if face recognition *were* accurate and unbiased.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: In addition to our analysis of facial recognition and the ethics thereof, I'm also glad that we were able to share detailed lessons from the process of operating the ethics board, which I hope will be useful to those working on/worried about various other technologies beyond FR.

text: I'm not sure what that might look like, though. There is probably also low hanging fruit in fine-tuning from generative models trained on various modalities. Will be very interesting to see how the science, economics, art, etc. of all of this plays out in the coming years! /Fin

author: Miles_Brundage
text: The simplest extrapolation would just be that, just as vision and NLP gradually matured to a point of being super commercially/creatively/etc. relevant over the course of many years, multimodal stuff combining vision+NLP might eventually reach that point + follow a similar path.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: E.g. folks pointed out that RL is maybe the wrong level/domain of analysis, and maybe there is insufficient commonality across RL tasks people care about for this to make sense, etc... But in any case, I suspect more will happen in this vein beyond vision and NLP.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: I've been thinking a bit about the growing practice of fine-tuning generic pretrained models: first in computer vision, now NLP (highly recommend @seb_ruder's great article on this https://t.co/EbSSMPpbv0)...Last time I mentioned this, people were skeptical that RL would be next.

text: And even if returns were diminishing for data, there could be other increasing returns effects that matter in AI (e.g. network effects favoring incumbent social networks or a tendency for talented researchers to want to work together).

author: Miles_Brundage
text: And even if there isn't a general tendency towards increasing returns, there could be in specific troubling cases, so this is a matter worth continuing to attend to from various perspectives.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: If one had to place bets now, I think diminishing returns is the safer bet, as it's more consistent with most of the relevant empirical evidence and theoretical arguments. But I agree with Posner/Weyl that increasing returns *would* be worrying w.r.t centralization of power.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: My current (still evolving) view on this is that there is no single right answer to this - even right now it depends on the task/domain/measure of value etc., and all of these things will evolve over time as algorithms/compute/data/society change.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: While I was generally a fan of this chapter and the book more generally, I found Posner/Weyl's arguments to be a bit weak, and it's not obvious how to reconcile it with the more grounded Hestness et al. analysis, or to compare Posner/Weyl's view to other theoretical arguments.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: They say that, while returns to data might diminish in the context of a particular task, this isn't true as a general description of the marginal value of data, because tasks are constantly changing, and there are always new uses of data being found.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Along the way, Posner and Weyl suggest that returns to data are actually increasing, and that this has implications for how we govern data use. In particular, they argue against the diminishing returns perspective (referencing some work related to Hestness et al.).

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Second, consider the book Radical Markets by Posner and Weyl (https://t.co/5NR6rBkvVU). Very thoughtful book on a range of issues, including the economic/social role of data and how they might evolve in the future, with people getting more compensation for their personal data.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Which is to say that in order to improve your deep learning system's performance linearly (up to some limit determined by the hardness of the problem/data quality), you will need to use an exponentially growing amount of compute/data, all other factors being equal.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: First, consider "Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically" by Hestness et al. at Baidu - https://t.co/wWim0MVP2P Fantastic paper that shows clear empirical tendencies distinguishing different ML domains w.r.t. returns to data, with a common theme of log-linear returns.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: I don't think anyone serious would argue that literally all data had the same properties, but it is not unreasonable to suspect that there are patterns, such as diminishing or increasing returns, based on some argument, be it empirical, economic, etc. Let's consider 2 such views.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
To simplify a lot*, let's consider two ends of a spectrum, from those who think that, in general, data has diminishing returns, to those who think it generally has increasing returns.

*there are many subtleties to the nature of data creation, labeling, use, value, etc of course!

author: Miles_Brundage
text: For these sorts of reasons, there have been various efforts to theorize the marginal value of data by various people. Hence one hears about diminishing returns to data, data network effects, etc. But not all of these theories are consistent with one another.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: E.g. ML folks might want to know the relative value of investing in algorithmic vs. data-related improvements, and security/privacy researchers might want to know how an cyber attacker or authoritarian gov't would think about the value of different data so as to plan accordingly.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Many different groups currently care (or should care) about the marginal value of data question, including ML researchers, ML engineers, entrepreneurs making data-intensive products/services, policy-makers, security experts, privacy/civil rights activists, etc.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: I've been thinking about the marginal value of data lately. "How useful would more data be?" is an important question, with many technical/policy/ethical/economic/etc. dimensions. But I doubt there is a single answer to this Q, despite recent efforts to argue for one. (Thread)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: For example, if many people used the same 3D environments, it makes more sense to share models/fine-tune on new tasks in those environments. But so far transfer learning has been unimpressive in RL generally, in part due to brittleness re: change in the task.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: I think it will happen eventually, but unsure what it will look like since today RL is happening in a huge variety of domains. How much pretrained models help depends in part on how many people are building systems in that domain/modality.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: If BERT/GPT-2 etc. represent NLP’s ImageNet moment, in the sense of transfer from pretrained models providing value (paraphrasing @seb_ruder’s great article last year: https://t.co/EbSSMPpbv0), when if ever will RL have such a moment?

text: 5. Finally, Nilsson wrote tons of articles on AI's societal implications. Early on in my exploration of AI, I read all the think pieces on AI I could find in old AAAI/IJCAI proceedings, AI Magazine, etc. and Nilsson really stood out for his foresight and concern. RIP.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 4. The Quest for AI was one of the first historical books on AI I read, and it is an epic synthesis of technical knowledge, deep personal experience, archival history, and accessible explanations - no one else could have written that book.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: You should persevere if you have good heuristics saying you're close, but all things being equal, you should be skeptical of deep searches, given that your heuristics are imperfect. Setting the right depth penalty + heuristics is non-trivial, obvi., but it's a useful framework.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: ... traveled, as well as one's best approximation of how close you are to the end goal. That's what A* formalizes. More generally, one should consider both the costs of search (broadly defined) as well as some set of heuristics for proximity to one's goals. ...

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 3. A generalized version of A* is how I think about my research planning, among other things. Whether one is searching through a map or navigating a landscape of ideas/experiments/literatures, one should take into account both the distance (conceptual/spatial/temporal)...

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 2. A* is one of the first algorithms I and many other students learned when taking AI classes, and it's a great starting point for that purpose! It's easy to explain, has formal guarantees, and inspires endless variations.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 1. His A* algorithm is the ancestor of modern GPS navigation algorithms among other things I/you use on a regular basis. A* continues to be explored theoretically and tons of new variants/approximations/etc. are constantly introduced and deployed.

text: @paul_scharre So not nothing to see ethically, but perhaps "nothing to see" novelty wise (that is a case FT could make but hasn't), and in any case not a TON to see novelty wise. If the case is disturbing, that fact should also be, and I'd love an article about that!

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @paul_scharre There's TONS to see, debate, disagree with, etc. - I see an ethically problematic paper at least once a day. I'd just like to see more proportionate emphasis/contextualized framing/care regarding the consequences of bringing politicians into the mix in today's environment.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @paul_scharre Theoretically, it is possible this is the most egregious, problematic, over the line, proximate-to-Chinese-military, etc. AI project in the US - but FT gives us zero reason to think that's the case other than elaborating on a particular case, giving reason to suspect an agenda.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @paul_scharre As someone who skims abstracts/author affiliations of at least hundreds of new AI papers everyday, I can assure you that there is nothing mindblowing here to someone who follows these areas closely. It comes off more like "hey, FT discovered international collaborations exist."

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @paul_scharre This is happening in a larger context, but the authors do not seem much concerned about responsibly engaging with that context (e.g. the AI community), vs. scoring a political point against China.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @paul_scharre And explore/communicate those in an even-handed way. FT has repeatedly broached the issue not in an even-handed way but in the form of naming and shaming people with the backing of a Senator behind them, in a time of hostility against universities working with foreign students.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @paul_scharre Agree abstractly, but if I wanted to make progress on that, the way to go about it would be to start with an understanding of what norms in the AI community around openness are, how important specific papers are, how hard it is to prevent AI advances from diffusing, etc.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: And to continue the analogy, AlphaGo and Five are both willing to sacrifice individual heroes/areas in the service of the larger mission of winning, while humans often (for reasons of folk wisdom or human psychology) avoid giving up battles when they should.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Similarly, again, in the case of AlphaGo, we have some objective but imperfect measures of progress in Go, and humans have intuitive senses, but AlphaGo's human-unaware win probability model still yielded insights, and one can imagine different models adding still more insights.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: (P.S. even in the domain of win probabilities, this isn't the best way to estimate them, since Five is assuming that the other players are also Five/will play as such, vs. realizing they are humans with unique strategies - but one could do that, and this gives a rough sense)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Notably, win probability isn't necessarily the thing we ultimately care about, but we may care about it sometimes, and directly estimating it through something like this can add value over cruder measures like kills/gold.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Correct me if I'm wrong @Smerity but I think the numbers at the very top are kills, with Five on the left and OG on the right, and then if there's gold stuff below those numbers, it means that side is up by that much gold (~1k small, 10k big lead) - starts even by those measures.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Starts around an hour and 34 minutes in. Similarly, AlphaGo was often aware of the turning of the tide before humans were, which is an interesting case of AI being able to add value not just to action-level decision-making but also analysis of larger trends/patterns/etc.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: P.S. Hopefully journalists I know already know the following, but for the record, I am a fan of a lot of AI journalism, too. But it is important to call out irresponsible stuff like this when it happens, and this article is part of a broader and dangerous trend.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: - (related to 1 and 2) Panicked coverage of cherrypicked (public) papers that say things one could have already known about from other public sources, all packaged together into a scary narrative that makes this random batch of papers sound like the most important thing ever.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
The recent FT story on China/AI and the reaction to it tells us more about the state of AI journalism than it does about China/AI:

- overhyping the significance of specific papers

- AI journalism can be used by politicians for partisan ends such as drumming up fear of China.

text: @rcalo Which is...some work, for sure, but accessible to most people and much less work per unit of human-ish-looking output for an arbitrary-ish domain than was possible a few years ago.

@rcalo All I'm doing is picking a task (e.g. produce Trump-like tweets), finding that data (easy in the Trump case, which is part of why I picked it)/downloading it to the server, and pressing a few "play" buttons.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: @tdietterich @jjding99 I agree such things can fulfilll such purposes, but that seems to give the WH a bit too much credit IMO. If it were a priority, Trump himself should say literally anything about it.

Another salient fact is that the White House is chaotic right now, and policy can change at a moment’s notice. This means that people understandably don’t take stuff that has happened so far without Trump’s involvement v. seriously, as any achievements are extremely fragile. /Fin

And one of the salient facts of the situation is that out of the two levers of influence @jjding99 mentioned, one is basically at a standstill (STEM investment), and on the other (immigration), the Trump admin. has gone in the exact opposite direction from what experts recommend.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: And to be clear, I hope things improve in these respects, and things aren’t apocalyptic now w.r.t. US AI policy - lots of sensible stuff in recent WH statements + DOD’s AI strategy. But it’s important that people have a realistic understanding of the current situation/challenges.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: This. It’s not that a good national strategy would be bad; it’s that so far, the evidence suggests that anything coming from the WH right now wouldn’t be good or executed, + high level strategies obscure ongoing low level failure on immigration etc. https://t.co/z0XjcfMXCt

quoted.text: The US doesn't need a "National AI Strategy." It's a fluffy way for Trump admin to self-congratulate/pretend it's doing stuff while ignoring more important/difficult areas where gov. can play a role: revive the Office of Tech Assessment, invest in STEM edu., immigration reform

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
Finally, we only briefly referenced bias in the post, but this is also a huge issue. If language models are poised to scale up text production in a ton of domains, what biases will be propagated/cemented in the public sphere by these tools? See https://t.co/78WSfjSry2

/fin

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Third, this isn't just about social media platforms - language is the currency of interaction in a huge variety of domains of life, including school, work, etc. Are we prepared in those domains, too?

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Second, as many folks have noted, we already have some ways of addressing spam, abuse, etc. on social media platforms - but they aren't perfect, and they need to get better fast.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: And in my view, GPT-2 1.5B (and its ilk) can meaningfully reduce the human labor required to produce a give quantity of human-passable content in a huge variety of domains. Some human judgment required still to select prompt + pick an output, but much less per unit of text.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: As context, bias was briefly mentioned as one of the considerations factoring into our release decision yesterday but I'm not super clear on how large LMs fit into the existing way of thinking re: bias in NLP. Seems to me to have a mix of old, new, and scaled up concerns.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
1. "normal" NLP bias stuff (implicit sentiments, associations etc.) as it relates to generated text
2. "normal" stuff w.r.t. fine-tuning on downstream tasks
3. "high level"/"meta" level bias re: longer term structure in text beyond #1/2
4.  Coverage/ease of use in diff domains

author: Miles_Brundage
text: A thought related to large language models and their societal impacts - what are the relevant bias considerations w.r.t. big LMs? In my mind, there are a few buckets.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: 2. This debate isn't *just* about GPT-2 and how risky it is today, but how to proceed given real tradeoffs (e.g. between showing people what the risks are by letting them use it, vs. limiting misuse), and we should have that convo before the next phase of LMs are widely deployed.
